opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think the thing that struck me most was how much of a shift in mindset it required. With the earlier AlphaFold work, the problem was very cleanly defined: you have a protein sequence, you want its structure. But biology doesn't really happen with proteins in isolation. Proteins are binding to DNA, they're interacting with RNA, they're being modulated by small molecules, ions, all sorts of things. If you actually want to understand what's happening inside a cell, or design a drug, you need to see how all of those pieces come together.

So once you start thinking about modeling all of biomolecular space, you have to step back and ask what the right representation even is. A protein is a nice chain of amino acids, but a small molecule could be almost anything chemically. That pushed us toward much more general approaches. We moved to something closer to a generative, diffusion-based model that works at the level of atoms, rather than relying so heavily on protein-specific machinery. That was really exciting, because it meant the same model could reason about very different kinds of molecules in a unified way.

The other interesting part was seeing how much the different modalities helped each other. You might think training on all these different molecule types would dilute performance, but in practice there was a lot of transfer. Learning the general physics and chemistry of how atoms arrange themselves turned out to be useful everywhere.

And practically, the small molecule side mattered a lot to me, because that's where it starts connecting to drug discovery. Getting accurate predictions of how a potential drug sits in a protein's binding pocket, without needing a crystal structure first, opens up a very different kind of workflow. It moves things from "let's understand biology" toward "let's actually design things with it," and that's the part I find most exciting.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the most interesting thing, honestly, was how much of the problem turned out to be shared. When we started AlphaFold, it was very much a protein-folding system, and a lot of the architecture had protein-specific ideas baked into it – you know, the way we represented residues, the way the multiple sequence alignments were used, the geometry modules that were built around the backbone frames of amino acids. And the naive assumption would be that to go to RNA or DNA or small molecules, you'd need a different model for each, with its own inductive biases.

What we found with AlphaFold 3 was that you could actually strip a lot of that away. If you move to a representation that's much more generic – essentially just atoms and tokens, and let the model learn the chemistry rather than hand-coding it – then suddenly one system can handle proteins, nucleic acids, ligands, ions, covalent modifications, all at once. And that was surprising to me, because the intuition from a lot of structural biology is that these are quite different worlds. The physics of a small molecule binding in a pocket feels very different from a protein folding on itself. But at the level of the learning problem, it's really the same thing: you're predicting a joint distribution over 3D coordinates given some set of interacting components.

The other thing that was interesting was the shift to a diffusion-based approach for the structure module. With proteins alone, the explicit frame-based geometry worked beautifully. But once you have things like ligands, where there's no natural backbone, you want something more flexible. Diffusion gives you that – it operates directly on atom positions, it handles arbitrary chemistry, and it also captures uncertainty in a more natural way. So in a sense, broadening the scope of the problem forced us toward a simpler, more general architecture, which is a pattern you see a lot in machine learning.

And then the thing I find most exciting, coming from the drug discovery side, is that this is actually where biology happens. Proteins don't operate in isolation – they bind to DNA, they're regulated by RNA, they're modulated by small molecules. So being able to model those interactions together, rather than one piece at a time, is what makes this genuinely useful for designing medicines. It's not just a bigger benchmark. It's closer to the real question people care about.

astra-6.text:
What I find most interesting is that it shifts the question from “What does this protein look like?” to “How does this protein interact with other molecules?” A protein’s structure is hugely informative, but so much of biology happens through interactions—with DNA, with RNA, with small molecules.

And those are quite different kinds of molecules, so you’re asking whether one model can capture the principles that govern how they fit together. That’s a really compelling learning problem. If you can predict those interactions well, you start to get a much richer picture of biological function, and something that’s potentially much more useful for designing medicines.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find most interesting is that it changes the scope of the problem. With proteins, you’re asking how a particular sequence folds. Once you bring in RNA, DNA, and small molecules, you can start asking how these different components come together and interact. That gets you closer to the molecular machinery of a cell, where proteins are doing things in concert with other molecules.

And small molecules are particularly exciting because of the connection to drug discovery. It’s not just about predicting the shape of a protein; it’s about understanding how a molecule might bind to it. That’s a much more direct connection between a structural prediction and a question you’d want to answer when developing a medicine.
